title: PatternMiner: Automated Mathematical Discovery Through LLM-Guided Training and Interpretation of Small Models
authors: Michael Ruofan Zeng, Junaid Hasan, Xuanyu Yang, Emily Xia Meng, Henry Kvinge
abstract: There are several approaches to AI-driven mathematical discovery. One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. In PatternMiner, an LLM agent generates mathematical datasets based on an initial broad question, trains narrow machine learning models on them, uses interpretability techniques to extract patterns from these trained models, and uses these patterns to formulate conjectures. Once an initial conjecture has been formulated, PatternMiner instructs the agent to search for counterexamples using calls to mathematical software. If a set of counterexamples can be found, these are used as feedback for conjecture refinement or another round of training and interpretability. The conjecture progressively evolves through this iterative sequence with the agent allowed to try to prove it at any point. We describe the results of applying PatternMiner to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics. PatternMiner proves several new theorems related to Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan--Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. We end by analyzing the most common routes to conjecture generation that are used by PatternMiner in our case studies as well as documenting the most common failure modes.

infographic.key_insight: PatternMiner combines LLM reasoning with small-model training and interpretability to turn patterns in mathematical data into iteratively refined conjectures and proofs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The system illustrates how an LLM agent can coordinate data generation, model training, interpretation, and mathematical software in an automated discovery workflow.
method: Generate mathematical datasets from a broad question and train small models.
Interpret learned patterns to formulate conjectures.
Search for counterexamples, refine conjectures or retrain, and attempt proofs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics, the authors report several new theorems, including a restricted Kazhdan–Lusztig combinatorial invariance result.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify success rates or computational costs, leaving reliability and scalability beyond these case studies unclear.
infographic.paper_title: PatternMiner: Automated Mathematical Discovery Through LLM-Guided Training and Interpretation of Small Models

title: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit
authors: Konstantin Riedl, Justin Sirignano, Konstantinos Spiliopoulos
abstract: Solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) constitutes a core task in many engineering and scientific disciplines. Physics-informed neural networks and the deep Galerkin method effectively leverage machine learning models to approximate solutions of known PDEs by minimizing residuals corresponding to the PDE operator alongside external constraints. Although second-order optimizers are becoming increasingly popular for training neural networks (NNs) to solve PDEs and empirically outperform their first-order counterparts in both speed and accuracy, the convergence theory for training such models is essentially confined to first-order methods. In this paper, we close this gap and develop a convergence analysis for the regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton methods. As the number of hidden units tends to infinity, the training dynamics converge in probability, with explicit rates, to the solution of a deterministic limit equation involving a Newton neural tangent kernel operator associated with the PDE. Although the limiting kernel operator admits no spectral gap, we prove that, in the overparameterized limit, the PDE residual vanishes as training proceeds, and, under mild assumptions, the NN converges to the PDE solution. We further show that, provided a sufficiently small regularization parameter, the projection of the residual onto any fixed number of leading eigenfunctions decays exponentially fast, demonstrating that this hyperparameter acts as a spectral filter: it lifts the convergence rates of high-frequency components toward those of low-frequency ones, thereby mitigating the spectral bias inherent in gradient descent. Mathematical challenges arise from the implicit parameter update involving a linear system whose dimension increases with the NN width and, for Newton's method, a potentially indefinite Hessian, as well as from the PDE operator entering the kernel.

infographic.key_insight: In the infinite-width limit, regularized Newton and Gauss–Newton training drives PINN PDE residuals to zero despite the limiting kernel having no spectral gap.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory supports second-order optimization for neural PDE solvers and explains how regularization can mitigate gradient descent’s spectral bias.
method: Analyze regularized Newton and Gauss–Newton training as network width grows.
Derive deterministic limiting dynamics governed by a PDE-associated Newton neural tangent kernel.
Prove residual convergence and exponential decay on any fixed leading eigenspace for sufficiently small regularization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence guarantees with explicit width-limit rates, but no numerical benchmarks or datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees concern the overparameterized limit; finite-width implementations must also solve growing linear systems and, for Newton, handle potentially indefinite Hessians.
infographic.paper_title: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit

title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective
authors: Charalambos G. Makridakis
abstract: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.

infographic.key_insight: A variational and numerical-analysis perspective connects neural-network minimisation to classical principles for understanding stability and reliability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Strongly coercive variational formulations may guide the design of more stable, reliable, and potentially efficient neural-network methods for scientific computing.
method: Formulate machine-learning algorithms as nonlinear minimisation problems.
Interpret stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness for neural-network approximations.
Study how continuous variational structure governs approximation behaviour.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a mathematical framework but reports no datasets, numerical benchmarks, or quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits from stronger coercivity require problem-specific formulation and validation; the abstract does not establish practical optimisation gains.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective

title: Exact Integration of ReLU-type Neural Networks for Solving PDEs
authors: Shima Baharlouei, Ignacio Brevis, Reuben Menezes, David Pardo, Kristoffer G. van der Zee
abstract: Developing robust training methodologies for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with neural networks is crucial for reliable scientific computing. Piecewise-linear activations such as the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) are a convenient choice in this setting as their structure resembles classical piecewise-linear approximations. However, when the loss functional incorporates the spatial gradient of the network, as in the Deep Ritz method, numerical integration becomes problematic. Specifically, relying on standard integration techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo sampling) during training yields incorrect gradients, even as the number of integration points approaches infinity, leading to optimization failure. To overcome this limitation, we present an integration framework for single-hidden-layer ReLU networks that computes correct gradients when using Deep Ritz for PDEs or PINNs for first-order problems. Our approach employs the Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm to partition the physical domain into subdomains according to breaking hyperplanes underlying the ReLU network. By finding these hyperplanes exactly, our method can correctly integrate the gradients, ensuring the optimizer receives correct information. In this work, we further assemble the energy in matrix--vector form that allows all neuron interactions to be computed efficiently with vectorized operations, introduce an alternative approach termed Conforming Monte Carlo that is a stochastic version of the proposed method, and propose two stochastic training strategies to reduce complexity. Numerical results on two-dimensional domains demonstrate that our framework recovers optimal PDE solutions that standard stochastic sampling and other existing quadrature methods fail to capture.

infographic.key_insight: For single-hidden-layer ReLU networks, integrating over regions defined by activation breakpoints yields correct PDE-loss gradients that standard sampling can miss even with arbitrarily many points.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Geometry-aware integration can make neural PDE training more reliable when losses depend on spatial gradients, as in Deep Ritz and first-order PINNs.
method: Partition the domain along ReLU breaking hyperplanes using Sutherland–Hodgman clipping.
Assemble the energy in matrix–vector form for vectorized neuron interactions.
Introduce Conforming Monte Carlo and two stochastic training strategies to reduce complexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests on two-dimensional domains recover optimal PDE solutions that standard stochastic sampling and other tested quadrature methods fail to capture.
infographic.watch_item: The framework targets single-hidden-layer networks, and geometric partitioning may become costly as neuron count or spatial dimension increases.
infographic.paper_title: Exact Integration of ReLU-type Neural Networks for Solving PDEs

title: Two 3-Dimensional Coefficient Inverse Problems for Wave-like Equations With a Single Location of the Point Source
authors: Michael V. Klibanov, Jingzhi Li, Tian Niu
abstract: In this paper two long standing open questions are addressed for the first time. Those questions are about Lipschitz stability estimates and uniqueness theorems for two Coefficient Inverse Problems (CIPs) for 3-Dimensional wave-like Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with formally determined input data. We assume that a certain associated PDE is written in finite differences with respect to time t. The unknown coefficients depend on all three spatial variables. The key novelty here is that the input data for these CIPs are generated by only a single location of the point source at the moment of time {t = 0}. In the first CIP (CIP1) the unknown coefficient is the potential of a wave-like PDE. The second CIP (CIP2) is concerned with a far more challenging case when the unknown coefficient is involved in the principal part of the hyperbolic operator. In addition to Lipschitz stability and uniqueness results, numerical methods are developed for both CIPs. Their convergence analysis establishes the global convergence property of both numerical techniques. The latter is unlike the local convergence of conventional numerical procedures for CIPs. The method for CIP1 is tested computationally. Its extensive numerical testing for complicated media structures consistently demonstrates a very accurate performance of this method for noisy input data. The authors declare that artificial intelligence was not used for any part of this work.

infographic.key_insight: With an associated PDE discretized in time, the paper establishes Lipschitz stability and uniqueness for two 3D wave-equation coefficient inverse problems using data from a single point-source location.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results support recovering spatially varying material parameters from wave measurements without requiring multiple source locations.
method: Recover an unknown potential in CIP1 and a principal-part coefficient in CIP2.
Use time finite differences in an associated PDE to establish stability and uniqueness.
Develop numerical methods with global convergence guarantees for both problems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive CIP1 numerical tests on complicated media with noisy data and consistently high accuracy, but provides no quantitative metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees rely on the stated time-discretized formulation, and the abstract reports computational validation only for CIP1.
infographic.paper_title: Two 3-Dimensional Coefficient Inverse Problems for Wave-like Equations With a Single Location of the Point Source

title: EPRO: Robust Policy Optimization Through an Imperfect Execution-Policy Predictor
authors: Yibo Wang, Changyi Yang, Yuanxin Liu, Zhaoran Wang
abstract: RL for LLMs often separates rollout generation from policy training. Although the two numerical engines share model parameters, they can induce different policies. This creates a challenge beyond correcting a known training-inference mismatch: during learner updates, the execution policy corresponding to the current parameters cannot be directly observed. We view this as optimizing an unobserved execution policy through an imperfect predictor of its evolution. This perspective raises two fundamental questions: how can we estimate the execution policy's response to learner updates, and how much should we trust that estimate when optimizing the actual execution policy? We introduce Execution-Policy Robust Optimization (EPRO) to address these challenges. Starting from the observed rollout-time execution policy, we use training-policy changes to construct a differentiable predictor of the current execution policy, whose score yields Transported Score Centering (TSC). Our robust-improvement analysis reveals how prediction error limits the magnitude of reliably justified updates. For practical implementation, we introduce Policy Shift as an observable proxy for prediction risk and use Shift-Aware Soft Clipping (SSC) to attenuate risky updates. Across four Qwen3 model settings, EPRO achieves the highest average held-out accuracy among the compared methods on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: EPRO optimizes an unobserved execution policy through an imperfect predictor, limiting update strength when prediction risk is high.
infographic.engineering_relevance: EPRO addresses policy discrepancies between rollout and training engines that share model parameters in LLM reinforcement learning.
method: Predict the current execution policy from the observed rollout-time policy and training-policy changes.
Use the predictor’s score to derive Transported Score Centering (TSC).
Estimate prediction risk with Policy Shift and attenuate risky updates using Shift-Aware Soft Clipping (SSC).
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four Qwen3 model settings, EPRO achieved the highest average held-out accuracy among compared methods on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Policy Shift is only a proxy for prediction risk; the abstract does not establish how reliably it tracks error across execution engines.
infographic.paper_title: EPRO: Robust Policy Optimization Through an Imperfect Execution-Policy Predictor

title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning
authors: Shijin Gong, Kai Ye, Victor Chernozhukov, Xinyu Zhang, Chengchun Shi
abstract: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.

infographic.key_insight: GRPO’s U-statistic structure turns group-size selection from trial and error into a variance-ratio estimation problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive group sizes can improve policy-gradient accuracy and reasoning-model training with modest additional computational cost.
method: Express GRPO’s policy gradient using U-statistics to guide group-size selection.
Use a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for uncertainty in a potentially small denominator.
Analyze three sample-size regimes and implement a jackknife-based selection rule.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on synthetic Reasoning Gym tasks and real-world math and code benchmarks report lower policy-gradient mean squared error and better policy optimization than fixed-group-size baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Near-zero variance-ratio denominators make estimation delicate; the abstract does not quantify gains or computational overhead.
infographic.paper_title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning

title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
authors: Konstantinos Emmanouilidis, Ziqing Xu, Salma Tarmoun, Lachlan MacDonald, Rene Vidal
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.

infographic.key_insight: Large-learning-rate SGD can achieve accelerated O(T^-2) convergence for cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, despite stochastic gradient noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results motivate exploring suitably chosen large learning rates rather than treating classical curvature-based stability limits as absolute tuning constraints.
method: Analyze stochastic optimization trajectories under large stepsizes.
Establish accelerated convergence for linear predictors and two-layer neural networks.
Derive tighter stable-regime guarantees, including improvements for deterministic optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence guarantees and numerical experiments demonstrating practical benefits, but provides no datasets or quantitative experimental comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees concern specific model classes and cross-entropy loss; the abstract does not specify the assumptions or stepsize-selection rules needed for implementation.
infographic.paper_title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates

title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
authors: Xiaocheng Luo, Peng Xu, Zaifu Zhan, Xiangyu Duan
abstract: Latent reasoning enables LLMs to operate in continuous embedding space, yet existing methods suffer from deterministic inference that precludes exploration of diverse reasoning paths. While recent approaches inject stochasticity to restore exploration, we identify two fundamental limitations: \textit{uniform stochasticity} across all steps is suboptimal, and unconstrained perturbations disrupt reasoning coherence. We propose Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR), a framework with two complementary mechanisms that operate at different temporal granularities within the GRPO reinforcement learning framework. At the token level, Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation (ASM) dynamically adjusts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal, increasing exploration when the model is uncertain and preserving stability when confident. At the training level, Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning (TAST) progressively decays the base stochasticity level following a curriculum schedule. Through this dual-level design, DLaR establishes a hierarchical exploration-exploitation strategy that operates at both token and training levels. Extensive experiments on four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DLaR achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Code: \href{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}.

infographic.key_insight: DLaR balances exploration and coherence in latent reasoning by adapting stochasticity to model uncertainty and training progress.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For mathematical reasoning systems using continuous latent states, DLaR offers an uncertainty-aware alternative to deterministic inference or uniform noise injection.
method: Use Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation to adjust perturbations at each latent step through a confidence–entropy fusion signal.
Use Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning to progressively decay base stochasticity over training.
Combine both mechanisms within GRPO reinforcement learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution math benchmarks, DLaR reports the highest average performance among evaluated methods: 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational overhead or establish whether the gains extend to larger models or non-mathematical tasks.
infographic.paper_title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models

title: Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based Mathematical Optimization Modeling
authors: Ryoichi Takase, Xian Yeow Lee, Hikaru Tomonari, Masaya Tsunokake
abstract: Industrial optimization involves complex constraints, making optimization modeling difficult to automate. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored for generating optimization models from natural language, but their reliability in end-to-end settings remains limited, often producing non-executable, infeasible, or feasible but incorrect solutions. In this work, we study failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling by decomposing the process into three components: mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing datasets that target each aspect. Using these datasets, we analyze how different components relate to errors and find that they are associated with different types of failure, although these relationships are not always strong or consistent. Furthermore, while combining these components improves execution reliability, feasible but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode, suggesting a remaining gap between executability and correctness. These findings highlight limitations of current dataset designs and suggest the importance of data that better capture constraint completeness and formulation accuracy to enhance reliability.

infographic.key_insight: Combining mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge improves execution reliability, but feasible yet incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLM-generated optimization models need validation of constraint completeness and formulation accuracy, not just successful solver execution or feasibility.
method: Decompose optimization modeling into mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge.
Construct datasets targeting each component.
Analyze component-specific failures and the effects of combining components.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on the constructed datasets links different components to different error types, though these relationships are not always strong or consistent.
infographic.watch_item: Current dataset designs may inadequately capture missing constraints and incorrect formulations, limiting what execution-based evaluation can establish.
infographic.paper_title: Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based Mathematical Optimization Modeling

title: Barron Smoothness for Layers in Deep Neural Networks
authors: G. Welper
abstract: In order to bound approximation errors for deep neural networks, we split the problem into two steps: First the selection of optimal infinite width limits for each layer and second an optimal discretization of all layers to obtain finite sized networks. We show that in expectation, the latter problem is equivalently characterized by a layer wise generalization of Barron norms. Moreover, we provide an analysis of the optimization landscape and show that local minima are characterized by an equidistribution principle akin to similar ideas in adaptive spline and finite element approximation.

infographic.key_insight: Layer-wise generalizations of Barron norms characterize expected discretization error when converting infinite-width layers into finite neural networks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory offers a framework for allocating finite network capacity across layers to control approximation error.
method: Separate approximation into selecting optimal infinite-width layers and discretizing them into finite layers.
Characterize expected discretization error using layer-wise Barron norms.
Analyze local minima through an equidistribution principle analogous to adaptive spline and finite element approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical characterizations of discretization error and local minima, but no datasets, benchmarks, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish a practical algorithm for finding optimal infinite-width layers or globally optimal finite networks.
infographic.paper_title: Barron Smoothness for Layers in Deep Neural Networks

title: Efficient Data Fusion in Distributionally Robust Optimization
authors: Buse Şen, Aras Selvi, Jean Pauphilet, Daniel Kuhn
abstract: Decisions under uncertainty increasingly rest on fragmented evidence, such as samples from related but different populations, privacy-protected summary statistics, or complementary statistical descriptions of the same data. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) can fuse such evidence by constructing one ambiguity set per source and hedging against all distributions in the intersection of these sets. This fusion approach is less conservative than aggregating the sources into a single ambiguity set, but it is computationally demanding. Exact reformulations grow exponentially with the number of sources, and even deciding whether the intersection is nonempty is NP-hard. We show that fusion DRO admits an exact reformulation in which the ambiguity sets are coupled only through functional Lagrange multipliers. Restricting these multipliers to affine decision rules yields upper bounds that decompose across the ambiguity sets, are exact for quadratic losses over Wasserstein balls around Gaussian references, and provably dominate aggregation-based relaxations such as Minkowski sums and balls around mixtures. The approximations admit finite conic reformulations in important special cases and subgradient methods for weakly convex losses, which makes fusion DRO applicable to neural network training. In portfolio, newsvendor, and binary classification experiments, the affine approximation stays close to the exact value wherever the latter is computable, scales far better than exact methods, and outperforms aggregation-based benchmarks out-of-sample.

infographic.key_insight: Affine functional multipliers make distributionally robust data fusion scalable while providing upper bounds tighter than aggregation-based relaxations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports robust decisions and neural network training using fragmented evidence without collapsing distinct sources into one ambiguity set.
method: Represent each evidence source by an ambiguity set and optimize against their intersection.
Couple sets through functional Lagrange multipliers, then restrict these to affine decision rules for decomposable upper bounds.
Use finite conic reformulations in special cases or subgradient methods for weakly convex losses.
infographic.evidence_signal: Portfolio, newsvendor, and binary classification experiments report near-exact values where computable, better scaling than exact methods, and stronger out-of-sample performance than aggregation benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Affine bounds are not generally exact; exactness is established for quadratic losses over Wasserstein balls around Gaussian references.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Data Fusion in Distributionally Robust Optimization

title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
authors: David Krame Kadurha, Alessandro Zocca, Sandjai Bhulai
abstract: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.

infographic.key_insight: Decision-focused learning enables fast multistage repair decisions, achieving 14%–23% lower costs than the next-best evaluated policy when repair budgets bind.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports rapid power-network repair scheduling under uncertain, time-varying failures and may extend to other structurally similar multistage optimization problems.
method: Predict scores for the sub-decision that drives state transitions using a neural network.
Train on offline single-scenario solutions with a Fenchel–Young loss and perturbed optimization oracles.
Exploit structural conditions under which the scored sub-decision enters the stage objective linearly.
infographic.evidence_signal: On common evaluation paths for synthetic 5-bus and IEEE 14-bus networks, DFL led all evaluated policies under binding budgets; its 5-bus mean costs were 1.7%–1.8% above the exact optimum.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits depend on problem structure and operating constraints: without a repair budget, DFL did not outperform the near-sighted MPC baseline on the 14-bus network.
infographic.paper_title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling

title: FokasNets: Completing missing boundary data in Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Operators via the Global Relation
authors: Kyriakos C. Georgiou, Khemraj Shukla, Athanassios S. Fokas, George Em Karniadakis
abstract: We introduce FokasNets, a framework that combines Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and operators (PINOs) with the Global Relation (GR) formulation of the Fokas method (also referred to as the Unified Transform), for mixed boundary problems. The general framework considers lifted representations of the neural network models, where the Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed by construction and the neural network learns the interior correction. The Global Relation is used as an additional solve during training that provides the missing boundary conditions to the lifted neural network, making training more efficient and accurate in the interior and on the boundary. We develop the construction of FokasNets for elliptic and evolution PDEs (Fokas-PINNs), and the corresponding PDE solution operator problems (Fokas Operator Networks - FONets), using the Global Relation formulations for these PDE classes. Furthermore, we develop the necessary theoretical framework for FokasNets, including error and stability analysis and show that FokasNets are universal approximators. We provide comprehensive numerical experiments, using examples with manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks. Compared to standard PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets and their lifted versions, FokasNets achieve significant improvements in solution accuracy in the interior and boundaries, both for single PDEs and particularly for solution operators, where the improvement reaches multiple orders of magnitude and fixed threshold errors are reached faster during training.

infographic.key_insight: FokasNets use the Fokas method’s Global Relation to supply missing boundary data, improving physics-informed neural solutions and solution operators.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate boundary completion could improve PDE-based engineering models when only mixed or incomplete boundary information is available.
method: Use lifted neural representations that impose Dirichlet conditions by construction and learn interior corrections.
Add a Global Relation solve during training to recover missing boundary data.
Develop Fokas-PINNs and Fokas Operator Networks for elliptic and evolution PDEs, with error, stability, and universal approximation analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured-solution tests and literature benchmarks show accuracy gains over standard and lifted PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets, reaching multiple orders of magnitude for solution operators and error thresholds faster during training.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires a suitable Global Relation formulation and an additional training-time solve; the abstract does not quantify that solve’s computational overhead.
infographic.paper_title: FokasNets: Completing missing boundary data in Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Operators via the Global Relation

title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
authors: Jan Rohleff, Johannes Schropp
abstract: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.

infographic.key_insight: VAE-NLME combines neural posterior approximation with importance weighting to converge almost surely to stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a theoretically grounded route to AI-enabled nonlinear mixed-effects modeling for dose selection and individualized dosing.
method: Use a neural encoder to amortize approximation of the intractable posterior.
Establish almost-sure convergence to ELBO stationary points without exact encoder training.
Use the encoder as an importance-sampling proposal for sufficient statistics to target marginal-likelihood stationary points.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports convergence proofs for both algorithm variants, but no empirical datasets, benchmarks or runtime results.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence to stationary points does not guarantee finding a global maximum of the marginal likelihood.
infographic.paper_title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling

title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
authors: Mohit Tekriwal, Het Mankad, Naifeng Zhang, Keita Teranishi, Sahil Bhola, Daisuke Uchida
abstract: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

infographic.key_insight: Trustworthy AI-assisted formalization in scientific computing requires identifying layer-specific failure modes and expert interventions that restore mathematical soundness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Scientific software teams can use these lessons to guide AI-assisted proofs while accounting for the challenges of computational procedures and modeling transformations.
method: Study AI-assisted formalization across abstraction layers of the scientific computing software stack.
Analyze proof failures and the expert feedback needed to recover soundness.
Derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports cross-layer case studies evaluating numerical proof completion and failure causes, but provides no quantitative success rates.
infographic.watch_item: Success on self-contained pure mathematics problems may not transfer to scientific computing, where representations and modeling assumptions require expert scrutiny.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned

title: From NP-Hardness to Exact Tractability Through Sample Abundance
authors: Mojtaba Soltanalian
abstract: Additional observations can make exact optimization tractable without changing the objective or feasible set. We establish this phenomenon for noisy parity fitting, a worst-case NP-hard problem, with uniformly sampled rank-one sign tensor entries, independent fair factor signs and independent errors. For fixed interaction order $k\ge3$, $n$ signs per block, logarithmic mean degree and known channel biases, $O(n/(\log n)^{1/(k-2)})$ further readings of the same source suffice with high probability for exact optimization in $O(n\log^2 n)$ worst-case work. The leading coefficient is sharp for weak recovery by depth-$O(\log\log n)$ local estimators with independent reading marks. A common signed-field law determines the gain over the generating source, the number of tied optima and the dimension needed for later reweightings. The geometry of the remaining coordinates determines the sharp radius of local verification for high-scoring assignments with high probability.

infographic.key_insight: Extra observations can make worst-case NP-hard noisy parity fitting exactly tractable without changing its objective or feasible set.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For systems matching the paper’s sampling and noise assumptions, collecting more readings can enable exact optimization with near-linear computational work.
method: Analyze uniformly sampled rank-one sign tensor entries with independent fair factor signs and independent errors.
For fixed interaction order k ≥ 3 and logarithmic mean degree, add O(n/(log n)^(1/(k−2))) readings of the same source.
Use a common signed-field law to characterize gains, tied optima and reweighting dimension, and residual geometry to characterize local verification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical high-probability guarantees of exact optimization in O(n log² n) worst-case work and a sharp leading coefficient for weak recovery within a specified class of local estimators.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require known channel biases and specific sampling and independence assumptions; robustness to real-world deviations is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: From NP-Hardness to Exact Tractability Through Sample Abundance

title: Routing and Cache Retention for Multi-Turn LLM Inference: Theory and Implementation
authors: Sentao Miao, Tianjiao Nie, Yuan Zhou, Song Yuan, Yuanwei Lu, Yibo Zhu
abstract: Multi-turn AI agents execute iterative loops of large language model (LLM) inference and external tool calls, transforming cluster serving into a dynamic resource-allocation problem where routing and key-value (KV) cache retention jointly govern prefix reuse across inter-turn delays. We formulate a fluid approximation of this system and show that optimal admission, routing, and eviction are governed by endpoint-specific shadow prices for computation and memory together with session continuation values. Building on this structure, we propose an asymptotically optimal buffer-reserve policy that absorbs stochastic fluctuations using a vanishing share of capacity. To handle asynchronous arrivals, delayed load reports, and engine-local memory management in production clusters, we translate these principles into a practical controller named PARK, which pairs online projected subgradient price updates and one-turn migration lookahead with a local KV retention index ranked by expected reuse value per byte-epoch. In real GPU cluster experiments serving a 197-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on multi-turn software-engineering agent benchmarks (SWE and Terminal-Bench), PARK outperforms all five load-balancing and prefix-aware baselines across contrasting traffic regimes. On 16 H200 GPUs, PARK raises output throughput by $24.2\%$ over the strongest baseline ($336.9\%$ over round robin) on turn-intensive SWE trajectories and by $40.0\%$ over the strongest baseline ($63.3\%$ over round robin) on generation-intensive Terminal-Bench trajectories. Controlled single-replica ablations show that our retention index alone cuts prior-prefix token loss from $13.26\%$ to $2.17\%$ and increases throughput by $36.7\%$ over least-recently-used (LRU) eviction, while 128-GPU scale-up experiments sustain 50,789 to 67,363 output tokens/s across 16~replicas with prefix cache hit rates of $91.3\%$ to $97.4\%$.

infographic.key_insight: Jointly optimizing request routing and KV-cache retention improves multi-turn LLM serving by balancing compute and memory costs against future prefix-reuse value.
infographic.engineering_relevance: PARK translates this optimization into a practical controller for GPU clusters serving agents that alternate between LLM inference and external tool calls.
method: Derive admission, routing, and eviction rules from a fluid model using resource shadow prices and session continuation values.
Use a buffer-reserve policy to absorb stochastic fluctuations with an asymptotically vanishing capacity share.
Implement online price updates, one-turn migration lookahead, and cache retention ranked by expected reuse value per byte-epoch.
infographic.evidence_signal: With a 197B-parameter MoE model on 16 H200 GPUs, PARK improved output throughput over the strongest baseline by 24.2% on SWE and 40.0% on Terminal-Bench; 128-GPU experiments sustained 50,789–67,363 output tokens/s.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover one model and two agent benchmarks; broader deployment should validate reuse-value estimates and robustness to delayed load reports.
infographic.paper_title: Routing and Cache Retention for Multi-Turn LLM Inference: Theory and Implementation

title: Congestion-Aware Adaptive Routing for LLM Classification
authors: Yuan Guo, Stefanus Jasin, Chen-An Lin
abstract: Organizations use large language models (LLMs) to classify jobs that differ in uncertainty and the cost of errors. Querying additional models may improve accuracy, but it also incurs fees and increases congestion at shared servers. We study congestion-aware adaptive routing (CAAR) policies that adapt model selection and stopping decisions to observed outputs while accounting for the steady-state congestion they generate. The objective is to minimize the long-run average cost of misclassification penalties, query fees, and holding costs. We can represent CAAR policies as a mixture of decision trees, and derive exact holding costs for first-come-first-served servers with exponential service times and processor-sharing servers with general service times. We formulate a convex optimization problem with unique optimal model loads. Congestion prices capture the marginal system-wide holding costs of additional queries and guide routing and stopping decisions through a Bayesian dynamic program. We characterize optimal stopping decisions and identify models whose information does not justify their cost. A column-generation algorithm computes optimal CAAR policies and provides an explicit optimality-gap bound. We also bound the additional cost of limiting cascade depth relative to full-depth CAAR. Finally, under a common query-depth limit, cascades with a predetermined model order can be arbitrarily more costly than optimal CAAR, even when the order is randomized and stopping decisions adapt to observed outputs. Numerical experiments distinguish the benefits of adaptive model selection and congestion-aware design.

infographic.key_insight: Adapting both model choice and stopping to observed outputs and server congestion minimizes the modeled long-run cost of classification errors, queries, and waiting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared LLM classification services can use congestion prices to balance accuracy gains against query fees and system-wide delays.
method: Represent adaptive routing policies as mixtures of decision trees and optimize model loads via convex optimization.
Use a Bayesian dynamic program with marginal congestion prices to select models and decide when to stop.
Compute policies through column generation with an explicit optimality-gap bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments separating the benefits of adaptive model selection and congestion awareness, but gives no datasets or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Exact holding-cost formulas assume specific queueing models; deployment requires checking how well these assumptions match actual LLM serving behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Congestion-Aware Adaptive Routing for LLM Classification

title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness
authors: Ke Tan, Chong-Jun Li, Xu Guo
abstract: Problem-independent machine learning (PIML) is an effective computational approach that combines the finite element method with machine learning. PIML uses neural networks to learn the mapping from material distributions or element geometries to the numerical shape functions of substructures. This approach avoids repeated computation while preserving the conformity of the underlying finite element discretization, thereby significantly improving the efficiency of substructure-based finite element analysis. However, existing studies on PIML have primarily focused on numerical accuracy and computational efficiency, while rigorous theoretical analyses of its approximation errors are still limited. In this paper, we establish an error analysis framework for PIML from a classical finite element perspective, in which the numerical error is bounded in terms of the finite element discretization error and the network generalization error. Our analysis shows that, when only rigid-body displacement invariance is enforced, the resulting error estimate contains a learning-induced term that does not necessarily decrease under mesh refinement. To ensure convergence, we propose an improved PIML scheme with linear completeness. By using linear displacement field constraints to reconstruct the corresponding columns of the transition matrix, we ensure that the resulting numerical shape-function space contains the space of linear polynomials. We derive error estimates and establish convergence results of the improved scheme in the H1 and L2 norms. Numerical experiments verify the theoretical results and demonstrate that the improved PIML achieves optimal convergence rates, good generalization performance, and numerical stability.

infographic.key_insight: Enforcing linear completeness gives problem-independent machine learning (PIML) finite element spaces a convergence guarantee that rigid-body displacement invariance alone does not provide.
infographic.engineering_relevance: PIML can accelerate substructure-based finite element analysis by learning reusable numerical shape functions while preserving conformity and controlling approximation error.
method: Bound PIML error using finite element discretization error and network generalization error.
Reconstruct transition-matrix columns using linear displacement constraints to reproduce linear polynomials.
Derive H1- and L2-norm error estimates and convergence results.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments supporting optimal convergence rates, good generalization, and numerical stability, but gives no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Linear completeness addresses mesh-refinement convergence, but accuracy still depends on network generalization for the material distributions and geometries encountered.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness
